passage:
I'm Sudha, and I was nine when Chithi said it at the family lunch. "Why are you not more like Leela? She is first in class and she sits so nicely." Leela is my cousin, and she was sitting right there.
Everyone kept eating. I looked at my rice. My ears went hot, and it felt like something heavy in my chest. I did not say a word. That night I told my doll, "I'm not good like Leela."
Even now I remember the sentence better than the lunch. Leela told me later that she hated being compared too. That helped a little.

qa.q: How old was Sudha when Chithi made the remark at lunch?
qa.a: Sudha was nine.

qa.q: What was Sudha feeling when Chithi compared Sudha with Leela?
qa.a: Sudha felt hurt and inadequate. The hot ears, the heavy chest and telling the doll "I'm not good like Leela" show it.

qa.q: What could a grown-up at the lunch have done to help Sudha?
qa.a: A grown-up could have said something kind and specific about Sudha, or gently changed the subject. That would show that Sudha does not have to be like Leela.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Leela to sit there while the comparison was made?
qa.a: Leela probably felt uncomfortable and awkward, and later said that being compared hurt too. Being praised at Sudha's cost is not easy either.

grounding: A child is compared unfavourably with a cousin in front of everyone and is left feeling inadequate, carrying the sentence for years.

passage:
Teacher's note, Thursday. Dolma, class 5, has been quiet all week and drew herself very small in the corner of her art page. At break I sat beside her. She said, "Mama's friend said, 'Why are you not more like Tashi? He is so clever.' Tashi is my cousin. I think I am just the wrong one." Then she added, "When I broke the jar, Uncle said, 'Very clever.' Was I clever?" I said his words were not a compliment and that sarcasm can be confusing.
I asked her to tell me three things she does well. She listed drawing, feeding the dog and counting fast. I have asked Dolma's mother to come in next week.
Rukmini, class teacher

qa.q: What did Dolma draw in the corner of her art page?
qa.a: Dolma drew herself very small in the corner.

qa.q: What was Dolma feeling when she said "I am just the wrong one"?
qa.a: Dolma felt inadequate and sad, as if she did not measure up to her cousin. Drawing herself small shows how much the comparison had shrunk her.

qa.q: What did Rukmini do to help Dolma see herself differently?
qa.a: Rukmini explained that sarcasm is confusing and asked Dolma for three things she does well. She also asked Dolma's mother to come in next week.

qa.q: What might Rukmini have been thinking on seeing Dolma quiet all week and drawn so small on her art page?
qa.a: Rukmini was probably worried that something was troubling Dolma. That is why Rukmini sat beside her at break and later asked Dolma's mother to come in.

grounding: A child is compared unfavourably with a cousin and hears sarcastic praise, and feels inadequate, and a teacher helps her name her strengths.

passage:
At the parent-teacher meeting in the school hall, Rafiq sat beside his father while Manjula Ma'am opened his report card.
"Maths is improving," she began. "Rafiq worked hard on fractions."
His father sighed. "Improving. His cousin Imran got full marks. Why can't you be more like Imran, Rafiq? Such a genius you are, sixty-two."
Rafiq stared at his shoes. His ears turned red. He didn't hear anything else the teacher said.
Manjula Ma'am put down her pen. "Mr Qureshi, Rafiq started at forty. Sixty-two is a big jump. He stayed back for help three times this month. That tells me a lot about him."
Rafiq looked up, just a little.
On the way out, she stopped him. "Rafiq. You're not Imran. You're you. And you're getting better."

qa.q: What marks did Rafiq get in maths?
qa.a: Rafiq got sixty-two.

qa.q: What does Rafiq staring at his shoes with red ears suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt ashamed and small, taking the comparison and the sarcastic "genius" to heart.

qa.q: How did Manjula Ma'am help, and what could parents learn from it?
qa.a: She pointed out his real progress from forty and his effort, then told him he is himself, showing parents to compare a child with their own past, not a cousin.

qa.q: How might Rafiq's father see his own words?
qa.a: His father may have thought he was motivating Rafiq, not realising the sarcasm left him feeling inadequate.

grounding: A child hears why can't you be like your cousin and is left feeling inadequate, and a teacher offers another view.

passage:
Monday. Sabina brought home her test: seventy out of a hundred. Ammi glanced at it. "Wah, what a topper. Rafiq got ninety-five. Why can't you be more like your cousin?"
Sabina went to her room and didn't come for dinner.
Thursday. It was Rafiq's birthday. Sabina said she had a stomach ache and wouldn't go. In her notebook, under "My Family", she drew everyone big and herself tiny in a corner.
Saturday. Ammi found the drawing. She sat on Sabina's bed for a long time.
"Sabina, when I said 'topper', I was joking."
"You weren't," Sabina said quietly.
Ammi was silent. Then: "You're right. It was unkind. I'm sorry. Seventy was your best yet. You are not Rafiq, and I don't want you to be."
Sabina didn't answer, but she let Ammi hold her hand.

qa.q: What did Sabina score on the test?
qa.a: Sabina got seventy out of a hundred.

qa.q: What does Sabina's drawing show about how she felt?
qa.a: It shows she felt small and inadequate in her family, taking the comparison with Rafiq into how she saw herself.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what began to fix it?
qa.a: Ammi's sarcastic comparison hurt; seeing the drawing, she admitted it was unkind, apologised and praised Sabina's own progress.

qa.q: How did Ammi feel when she found the drawing?
qa.a: Ammi was shaken and regretful, sitting silently for a long time before apologising.

grounding: A child told why can't you be like your cousin takes the sarcasm literally and carries it into her self-image.

passage:
"Hansa, you asked why I never go to cousin Vikram's parties. Sit. Let your Mohit Chacha tell you something from when I was ten.
"Every Sunday we went to Vikram's house. And every Sunday my father said, 'Look at Vikram. First in class, first in cricket. Why can't you be more like him?' Once he said, 'Mohit is our family's great scientist,' after I failed science, and everyone laughed.
"I didn't laugh. I believed him. I thought I was the stupid one in the family.
"I stopped trying in science. Why try, if I was stupid?
"Years later, a college teacher saw my drawings and said I had a real eye. I'm an architect now, Hansa. But even today, at forty, when I see Vikram, some part of me is ten again, standing in that drawing room.

qa.q: What did Mohit's father say after he failed science?
qa.a: He said, "Mohit is our family's great scientist," and everyone laughed.

qa.q: How did young Mohit feel when everyone laughed?
qa.a: Young Mohit felt humiliated and inadequate, believing he really was the stupid one in the family.

qa.q: What was a turning point inside the story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: A college teacher praised his drawings, which gave him a different picture of himself than the one his father's comparisons had built.

qa.q: How might Vikram have experienced those Sundays?
qa.a: Vikram may have felt awkward or uneasy being held up as the example, even if he enjoyed the praise.

grounding: An elder recalls being compared with a cousin and mocked, and how it shaped his self-image for years.

passage: The power had gone in the Kanpur flat, and with the fan dead Mummy fanned herself with a newspaper while she read Manoj's report card. "Wah. Sixty-one in maths. Very impressive." Manoj started to smile, then saw her face. "Why can't you be more like your cousin Harshita? Ninety-four, and she does dance class too." Manoj went to the balcony and sat with his knees up in the heat. Next day, when Hafsa asked for help with fractions, he shook his head. "Ask someone else. I'm the dumb one in my family." Hafsa stared. "You taught me long division last month." Manoj just shrugged and kept his notebook closed.

qa.q: What did Manoj get in maths?
qa.a: Sixty-one in maths.

qa.q: Why did Manoj start to smile and then stop?
qa.a: Manoj first took "very impressive" literally and felt pleased, then saw Mummy's face, caught the sarcasm and felt ashamed and not good enough.

qa.q: What could Mummy say instead when a mark disappoints her?
qa.a: Speak plainly and without comparison, like "Maths looks hard this term; which part felt tricky?", and leave Harshita out of it.

qa.q: How might Hafsa see Manoj calling himself "the dumb one"?
qa.a: Hafsa is surprised and puzzled, since Manoj taught her long division last month; she can see he now believes something untrue about himself.

grounding: Shows a child who hears sarcasm and a comparison with a cousin and carries the feeling of not being good enough into how he sees himself.
